name: Survodutide

b.x: 62% of MASH patients improved in under a year, without their fibrosis getting worse. That's the headline number from the Phase 2 MASH trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine (n=293) [1]. Survodutide (BI 456906) is a dual glucagon and GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by Boehringer Ingelheim. It works two angles at once: GLP-1 receptor activation suppresses appetite and slows gastric emptying, while glucagon receptor activation drives hepatic fat oxidation and thermogenesis. Compared to semaglutide and tirzepatide, survodutide adds the glucagon receptor arm those two lack, which is why its early data centers on liver fat. The MASH trial at 4.8 mg weekly showed 62% of participants improved in MASH without worsening of fibrosis at 48 weeks, versus 14% on placebo. Fibrosis improved by at least one stage in 36%, and liver fat dropped by at least 30% in 67% of participants. A separate Phase 2 obesity trial (Lancet 2024, n=387) [2] landed on 18.7% weight loss at 46 weeks with the same 4.8 mg dose. Phase 3 obesity results landed in 2026. SYNCHRONIZE-1 (NCT06066515) enrolled adults without diabetes. At 76 weeks, 3.6 and 6.0 mg produced 12.2% and 13.0% weight loss vs 5.4% on placebo (NEJM 2026) [4]. SYNCHRONIZE-2 (NCT06066528, n=752) enrolled adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, who lost 8.2% and 9.8% vs 3.9% (NEJM 2026) [5]. Both counted everyone randomized. Neither is a MASH trial; the MASH Phase 3, LIVERAGE (NCT06632444), is still recruiting. One wrinkle worth knowing: Phase 2 turned up a non-linear dose response for MASH. The 6.0 mg arm actually had worse MASH improvement than 4.8 mg (43% vs 62%). Whether that pattern holds in Phase 3 will matter. The compound is not FDA-approved, not commercially available, and carries the usual GLP-1 class GI burden. About 75% of Phase 2 participants reported gastrointestinal side effects.

Survodutide activates two receptors that complement each other. GLP-1 receptor agonism suppresses appetite through hypothalamic signaling, slows gastric emptying (which extends satiety), and boosts glucose-dependent insulin secretion. That side of the molecule handles the appetite and blood sugar piece. The glucagon receptor component does something GLP-1-only drugs cannot. Glucagon receptor activation increases hepatic fat oxidation, converting stored liver fat into energy. It also raises energy expenditure through thermogenesis and promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue. This is the mechanism behind the dramatic liver fat reduction in the MASH trial. A C18 diacid modification on the peptide enables albumin binding in the bloodstream. That extends the half-life to approximately 6 days, making weekly subcutaneous dosing practical. The dual-receptor approach creates a built-in counterbalance: GLP-1 lowers blood glucose while glucagon tends to raise it. In clinical trials, the net effect on fasting glucose was neutral to mildly favorable in non-diabetic participants, with no significant hypoglycemia reported.
Survodutide benefits center on liver fat reduction and metabolic weight loss through its dual GLP-1/glucagon mechanism.
62% of MASH patients improved in MASH without worsening of fibrosis at 4.8 mg weekly, and 67% had at least a 30% drop in liver fat (NEJM 2024, n=293) [1].

Weekly dosing from a single subcutaneous injection, enabled by C18 diacid albumin-binding modification with a half-life of approximately 6 days.
Glucagon receptor-driven thermogenesis adds an energy expenditure component that pure GLP-1 agonists lack; this may explain the particularly strong liver fat results.

No Phase 3 MASH biopsy results yet (LIVERAGE is recruiting). Phase 2 MASH trial had non-linear dose-response: 4.8mg outperformed 6.0mg for improvement in MASH (62% vs 43%). Long-term safety >48 weeks uncharacterized. Not FDA-approved.

Survodutide requires a 10 mg vial and 2 mL bacteriostatic water for reconstitution. That gives you 5 mg/mL, or 5,000 mcg/mL. On a standard U-100 insulin syringe, each unit equals 50 mcg. So 0.6 mg (the starting dose) is 12 units. The 1.2 mg escalation dose is 24 units. At the full 4.8 mg MASH target, you're drawing 96 units. The thing most people miss about survodutide is the escalation timeline. You're looking at 40 weeks of dose escalation before reaching therapeutic range. That's nearly 10 months. The clinical trials built this in deliberately because the GI burden is dose-dependent; skipping steps causes severe nausea and vomiting. If you need to pause dosing for more than 2 weeks, restart from 0.6 mg and re-titrate. That's the clinical trial protocol, not optional caution. Store reconstituted vials at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius and use within 4 weeks.
Cycling Protocol
Based on SYNCHRONIZE Phase 3 trial design (76 weeks). Titrate from 0.6mg weekly over 20 weeks. Long-term maintenance data not yet available.
Survodutide Continuous

No cycling data exists. Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE treats survodutide as continuous 76-week therapy with no off periods. Weight regain upon discontinuation is expected (consistent with GLP-1 class). Long-term maintenance protocols post-76 weeks are not yet established.

Reconstitute one 10 mg vial with 2.0 mL bacteriostatic water. Aim the stream at the glass wall, not directly onto the powder. Swirl gently until dissolved. This yields 5,000 mcg per mL (50 mcg per insulin syringe unit).

Draw your dose using a U-100 insulin syringe with a 29 to 31 gauge needle. Starting dose: 12 units (600 mcg / 0.6 mg). Escalation schedule: 24 units at week 9 (1.2 mg), 36 units at week 17 (1.8 mg), 48 units at week 25 (2.4 mg), 72 units at week 33 (3.6 mg).
At the 6.0 mg Phase 3 target dose, you'll need 120 units (a full 1 mL draw). Use a 1 mL syringe or split into two 0.5 mL draws from the same vial.

Survodutide's dominant safety signal is gastrointestinal toxicity. In the Phase 2 obesity trial, approximately 75% of participants on survodutide reported gastrointestinal side effects. Nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting were the most common, and they followed a predictable pattern tied to dose escalation. Each step up in dose triggered a new wave of GI symptoms that typically settled within 2 to 4 weeks at a stable dose level. The frequency data from Phase 2 breaks down as follows. Nausea was common (reported in more than 40% of participants at 4.8 mg). Diarrhea affected roughly 20 to 30%. Vomiting occurred in approximately 15 to 25% depending on the dose arm. Decreased appetite was frequent but often welcomed by participants in the obesity trial. Constipation showed up at higher doses as well. One safety point that deserves attention: the GLP-1 receptor agonist class carries a boxed warning in approved compounds (semaglutide, tirzepatide) for thyroid C-cell tumors observed in rodent studies. This signal has not been confirmed in humans, but survodutide belongs to the same class. Thyroid monitoring at baseline is warranted. Pancreatitis is a class concern. Any episode of persistent, severe abdominal pain should prompt lipase and amylase testing and immediate discontinuation if pancreatitis is confirmed. For people with type 2 diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas, adding survodutide raises hypoglycemia risk. The glucagon component partially offsets this in non-diabetic users, but the combination with exogenous insulin removes that safety margin. Contraindications include personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN2), history of pancreatitis, pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe gastrointestinal disease such as gastroparesis, and decompensated cirrhosis. A dedicated pharmacokinetic study [3] confirmed that survodutide's PK is not significantly altered by cirrhosis, but safety data in decompensated (Child-Pugh C) cirrhosis is insufficient. If GI effects are disproportionately severe at the 0.6 mg starting dose, suspect inaccurate vial concentration from grey-market sourcing. A certificate of analysis is the only way to check the batch.
Common Issues & Solutions
Nausea peaks at each dose escalation step: reduce escalation pace (extend current dose by 4 additional weeks) rather than stopping. Most GI effects resolve within 2–4 weeks at a stable dose.
Phase 2 showed 6.0mg had WORSE MASH improvement than 4.8mg (43% vs 62%): for liver endpoints specifically, higher dose is not better. Target 4.8mg for MASH, not 6.0mg.
Vomiting during titration: switch injection to evening before sleep. Pre-medicate with ondansetron for escalation weeks if GI tolerance is consistently poor.
If dosing is interrupted >2 weeks, restart from 0.6mg and re-titrate: matches clinical trial protocol and minimizes rebound GI effects.

Grey-market purity variance: if GI effects are disproportionately severe at low doses (0.6mg), suspect overdose from inaccurate concentration. Only a CoA can confirm the batch; consider reconstituting with more BAC water.

Survodutide is an investigational drug. It is not FDA-approved for any indication as of October 2026. No New Drug Application (NDA) filing has been officially confirmed by Boehringer Ingelheim. The compound is still in Phase 3 development. SYNCHRONIZE-1 (NCT06066515, obesity without diabetes) and SYNCHRONIZE-2 (NCT06066528, obesity with type 2 diabetes) are completed and were published in NEJM in 2026. The MASH Phase 3, LIVERAGE (NCT06632444), is recruiting. Survodutide is not available through compounding pharmacies under 503A or 503B pathways. Any product marketed as survodutide is a research chemical sold without regulatory oversight. Pricing from unvetted grey-market sources ranges from $95 to $290 per 10 mg vial. Purity and dosing accuracy cannot be guaranteed. Request HPLC and mass spectrometry certificates of analysis; the peptide molecular weight is approximately 4,232 Da. WADA's 2026 Prohibited List does not name survodutide or any other GLP-1 receptor agonist. Survodutide has no regulatory approval, so it may fall under section S0 (non-approved substances), which WADA prohibits in and out of competition. Athletes subject to anti-doping testing should check with their anti-doping organization before use. This content is for educational and research purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any investigational compound.

faqs.q: What makes survodutide different from semaglutide for liver disease?
faqs.a: The glucagon receptor component directly drives hepatic fat oxidation: something GLP-1-only drugs can't do on their own. In the Phase 2 MASH trial, survodutide 4.8 mg improved MASH without worsening fibrosis in 62% of participants, versus 14% on placebo. Semaglutide's liver fat effects are largely a side benefit of weight loss.

faqs.q: Why does Phase 3 go up to 6.0 mg when Phase 2 maxed at 4.8 mg?
faqs.a: Weight loss hadn't plateaued at 46 weeks with 4.8 mg in the Phase 2 obesity trial. Boehringer Ingelheim selected 6.0 mg for Phase 3 to see if they can push efficacy further. In SYNCHRONIZE-1, 6.0 mg produced 13.0% weight loss at 76 weeks vs 12.2% on 3.6 mg and 5.4% on placebo (NEJM 2026, PMID 42253238).

faqs.q: Does the glucagon component cause blood sugar problems?
faqs.a: No: therapeutic glucagon receptor agonism at these doses primarily increases hepatic fat oxidation and energy expenditure, not blood glucose. The GLP-1 component provides a glucose-lowering counterbalance. Clinical trials showed no significant hypoglycemia in non-diabetic participants.

faqs.q: Which dose should I reference when looking at survodutide data?
faqs.a: It depends on the goal. For weight, Phase 3 tested 3.6 mg and 6.0 mg over 76 weeks. People without diabetes lost 12.2% and 13.0% vs 5.4% on placebo (SYNCHRONIZE-1). People with type 2 diabetes lost 8.2% and 9.8% vs 3.9% (SYNCHRONIZE-2). For MASH, 4.8 mg still has the best biopsy data: 62% improved without worsening fibrosis in Phase 2. The MASH Phase 3, LIVERAGE, hasn't reported yet.

faqs.q: What does the "decompensated cirrhosis" contraindication mean in practice?
faqs.a: Survodutide's pharmacokinetics aren't significantly changed by cirrhosis (confirmed by a dedicated PK study). But safety data in decompensated cirrhosis (meaning Child-Pugh C with ascites, encephalopathy) is insufficient. The drug may be appropriate in compensated cirrhosis with monitoring, but is off-limits when liver function is severely compromised.

Survodutide rates a B on the Peptide Schedule safety scale, and gastrointestinal toxicity is the dominant signal. Roughly 75% of Phase 2 participants reported GI side effects, tied to each step of the unusually long 40-week titration, then settling within 2 to 4 weeks at a stable dose. It is subject to the GLP-1 class thyroid C-cell concern and is not FDA-approved.
Survodutide typically comes in 10mg vials. Add 2mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Survodutide?
faqs.a: The half-life of Survodutide is ~6 days. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: 62% of MASH patients improved in 48 weeks without their fibrosis getting worse. That result, from a 2024 NEJM trial of 293 patients, put survodutide on the map as a dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist built for metabolic liver disease. Boehringer Ingelheim's Phase 3 obesity trials (SYNCHRONIZE-1 and -2) reported 9.8 to 13.0% weight loss on 6.0 mg at 76 weeks in 2026. The compound also produced 18.7% body weight loss at 46 weeks in a separate Phase 2 obesity trial. It isn't FDA-approved, and the 40-week dose escalation schedule is slow by any standard. For people tracking MASH therapies or next-generation weight loss agents, survodutide is one to watch closely.
